signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: How is a pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) classically defined?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: A fever >38.3°C on several occasions for >3 weeks that remains undiagnosed after initial appropriate inpatient / outpatient investigation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What are the four broad categories of PUO?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back:
• Infection
  • malignancy
  • connective-tissue (autoimmune / inflammatory) disease
  • and miscellaneous (e.g. drug fever, PE, thyroid)
— with a proportion undiagnosed.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What must be excluded immediately in any febrile patient before a staged PUO workup?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back:
• Sepsis (fever + organ dysfunction → Sepsis 6)
  • meningococcal disease (non-blanching rash)
  • and neutropenic sepsis (recent chemotherapy).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What is neutropenic sepsis and how quickly is it treated?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: Fever with neutropenia (usually within weeks of chemotherapy); a medical emergency treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour, without waiting for the count.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: Which malignancies most classically cause fever / night sweats / weight loss (B symptoms)?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: Lymphoma and leukaemia (and renal cell carcinoma) — the fever is part of the B-symptom cluster.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: Which infective causes should be considered in a persistent fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back:
• TB
  • infective endocarditis
  • occult / deep abscess
  • osteomyelitis
  • and infections in the returning traveller (malaria, enteric fever).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What is the immediate management of sepsis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: The Sepsis 6 within one hour: take blood cultures, lactate and urine output; give oxygen, IV fluids and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: Why is a non-blanching purpuric rash with fever an emergency?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: It suggests meningococcal septicaemia; give parenteral antibiotics (e.g. IM/IV benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone) immediately without delay.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What key exposures must be asked about in a fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back:
• Travel, prophylaxis and insect bites
  • animal, food and water contact
  • sexual history
  • IV drug use
  • prosthetic material / valves
  • and immunosuppression.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: Name investigations in a staged PUO workup beyond first-line bloods and cultures.
Why should empirical antibiotics generally be avoided in a stable PUO?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: They can mask the underlying diagnosis (partially treated infection, culture-negative endocarditis) and delay it — investigate systematically instead.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.front: What is the significance of fever in a returning traveller?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.back: It is malaria until excluded (blood films ×3); also consider enteric fever, dengue, viral haemorrhagic fever and hepatitis, guided by the itinerary.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: What magnitude of unintentional weight loss is clinically significant?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back: Loss of >5% of body weight over 6–12 months (or any unexplained, progressive loss) warrants investigation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: Which weight-loss features constitute a cancer red flag?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back: Weight loss with anorexia, night sweats, a mass or lymphadenopathy, or with dysphagia, change in bowel habit, PR bleeding or haemoptysis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: How does weight loss from hyperthyroidism differ from most other causes?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back:
It occurs despite a normal or increased appetite, with
  • heat intolerance
  • tremor
  • palpitations
  • sweating
  • and diarrhoea.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: Which endocrine emergency-prone condition presents with weight loss plus polyuria and polydipsia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back: New diabetes mellitus (especially type 1), which can progress to diabetic ketoacidosis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: What GI condition causes weight loss with steatorrhoea and bloating?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back: Malabsorption — classically coeliac disease (also pancreatic insufficiency, IBD, bacterial overgrowth).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: Which infections classically cause weight loss with fever and night sweats?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back:
• Depression (with low mood and anhedonia)
  • eating disorders (fear of weight gain, distorted body image)
  • and substance misuse.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: What baseline blood panel is appropriate for unexplained weight loss?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back:
• FBC
  • U&E
  • LFTs
  • calcium
  • glucose / HbA1c
  • TFTs
  • coeliac serology (tTG)
  • CRP / ESR
  • and an HIV test
  • plus a chest X-ray.
A malignancy-associated metabolic state of anorexia, weight loss and muscle wasting driven by cytokines, not simply reduced intake.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: Why must weight loss not be attributed to depression or old age too readily?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back: Because malignancy, TB / HIV and treatable metabolic disease can be missed, leading to late and dangerous diagnoses.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.front: Which cancers commonly present with weight loss?
What supportive measures accompany treating the cause of weight loss?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.back:
• Nutritional assessment (MUST)
  • dietetic input with oral supplements / feeding routes
  • and treating reversible contributors.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: What red-flag features suggest a sinister cause of fatigue?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: Weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, or easy bruising / bleeding — pointing to malignancy or haematological disease.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: What is the commonest single cause of fatigue presenting to primary care?
What baseline screening bloods are appropriate for unexplained fatigue?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: Fatigue with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes; confirm with TFTs.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: Which haematological cause of fatigue presents with pallor and exertional breathlessness?
What sleep disorder causes fatigue with snoring and daytime somnolence?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: Obstructive sleep apnoea — assess with a sleep study.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: What is required to diagnose chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS)?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: Persistent, disabling fatigue (typically >3 months) with post-exertional malaise, made only after excluding other causes — a positive diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: Which endocrine emergency can present as fatigue with postural dizziness, pigmentation and hyponatraemia?
Which malignancy causes fatigue with bone pain, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: By low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite disturbance and diurnal variation, screened with tools such as the PHQ-9.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.front: What is a safe minimum assessment for a fatigued patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fatigue / Tir.back: A focused history and examination plus a screening blood panel, with red flags investigated and mood assessed.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: Why is malaise particularly important in the frail elderly?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: In the frail elderly it may be the only sign of serious illness — occult sepsis or a metabolic emergency — in a patient who may not mount a fever.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: Which metabolic emergencies can present as non-specific malaise?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: DKA / HHS, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, an Addisonian crisis and uraemia — so check glucose, U&E and calcium.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: What bedside and blood tests should be done early in an unwell, malaise-only elderly patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back:
• Observations (NEWS2)
  • capillary glucose
  • and bloods including FBC, U&E, calcium, CRP ± cultures and a venous gas.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: Which viral infections cause malaise with sore throat, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: EBV (glandular fever) and CMV; also HIV seroconversion and viral hepatitis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: What triad suggests an Addisonian crisis behind malaise?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: Malaise with anorexia, constipation, polyuria, confusion — “bones, stones, groans and psychiatric moans”.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: Which endocrine causes of malaise should be screened?
How can uraemia / CKD present as malaise?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: Malaise with nausea, pruritus, anorexia and reduced urine output; U&E confirms.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: Which iatrogenic causes of malaise are common?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: With low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and reduced energy; screened clinically.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: What is the danger of labelling a run-down elderly patient as “just tired”?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: It risks missing occult sepsis or a metabolic emergency — observations and basic bloods are mandatory.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.front: What is a sensible first blood screen for undifferentiated malaise?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Lethargy & Ma.back: FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, glucose, CRP and TFTs, adding cortisol, monospot / viral serology and HIV as indicated.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: Enlarged lymph nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions — distinct from a single or regional (localised) node.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: Which malignant causes must be excluded in generalised lymphadenopathy?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: Lymphoma (painless rubbery nodes + B symptoms) and leukaemia (nodes with cytopenias / bruising).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: What is the correct biopsy for a suspected lymphomatous node?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: An excision node biopsy (to preserve architecture) — not a fine-needle aspirate.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: Which infective causes commonly produce generalised lymphadenopathy?
Which immunological / inflammatory conditions cause generalised lymphadenopathy?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: Tender, mobile, small nodes with a viral prodrome are usually reactive; hard, fixed, non-tender, >2 cm, matted or supraclavicular nodes are concerning.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: What are the classic B symptoms of lymphoma?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back:
• Fever
  • drenching night sweats
  • and unexplained weight loss (>10% in 6 months).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: Which node location is especially concerning for malignancy?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: A supraclavicular node (e.g. Virchow’s node) — often signifies thoracic or abdominal malignancy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: What core investigations are used in generalised lymphadenopathy?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back:
• FBC + blood film
  • monospot / EBV serology
  • HIV test
  • LDH
  • CRP / ESR
  • a chest X-ray
  • autoantibodies
  • and an excision node biopsy for persistent nodes.
A young adult with sore throat, fever, cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; avoid amoxicillin (rash).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.front: How long should a reactive-appearing node be observed before biopsy?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised L.back: Persistence beyond about 4–6 weeks (or any suspicious features) warrants urgent referral and biopsy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: They are drenching — soaking nightclothes and bedding — and persistent, rather than mild transient sweating.
Lymphoma and leukaemia (as part of B symptoms), and other haematological malignancies.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: What is the commonest benign cause of night sweats in women?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: The menopause (vasomotor symptoms), with hot flushes and menstrual change.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: How can diabetes treatment cause night sweats?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: Nocturnal hypoglycaemia — sweats with a morning headache, relieved by eating.
SSRIs, opioids, and others; alcohol and its withdrawal also cause sweats.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: What accompanying features make night sweats a red flag?
What investigations are appropriate for unexplained drenching night sweats?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: FBC + film, LDH, CRP / ESR, blood cultures, a chest X-ray, HIV test and TFTs, with CT / node biopsy if B symptoms are present.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: How does endocarditis present with night sweats?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: Night sweats and fever with a new murmur, splinter haemorrhages and other embolic phenomena.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: Why should drenching night sweats with weight loss not be dismissed as stress or menopause?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: Because lymphoma, TB and endocarditis can be missed; the red-flag cluster demands investigation first.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.front: Which single test should be offered in unexplained systemic night sweats?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Night Sweats.back: An HIV test (alongside a search for TB and malignancy).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: Why is a new loss of appetite important in older people?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back: It can be an early, non-specific sign of serious organic disease — malignancy, occult sepsis or a metabolic upset — not simply “old age”.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: How does loss of appetite differ from anorexia nervosa?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back: Here anorexia means reduced desire to eat as a symptom of disease; anorexia nervosa is a psychiatric eating disorder with fear of weight gain and distorted body image.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: Which malignant syndrome links anorexia and weight loss?
Which metabolic derangement causes anorexia with constipation and confusion?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back: It causes anorexia with nausea, pruritus and a metallic taste; U&E confirms renal impairment.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: Which GI conditions cause anorexia with early satiety and weight loss?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back: Gastric cancer, peptic ulcer disease and other upper-GI pathology.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: Which psychiatric condition is a leading cause of anorexia?
What tool screens nutritional risk in a patient with poor appetite?
What should always be done to objectively assess appetite loss?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back:
• Weigh the patient
  • calculate BMI / MUST
  • and quantify actual intake.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.front: Which endocrine cause presents with anorexia, weight loss, pigmentation and hyponatraemia?
What supportive management accompanies treating the cause of anorexia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Loss of Appet.back:
• Dietetic input
  • oral nutritional supplements
  • and appropriate feeding routes
  • plus treating reversible contributors.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: Why are falls in older adults described as multifactorial?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: Because several interacting factors (cardiac, neurological, medications, vision, MSK, environment) usually combine to cause them.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: What is the single most important question in assessing a fall?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: Whether there was a true loss of consciousness — which raises syncope.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: Which cardiac causes of a syncopal fall must be excluded?
What investigation is mandatory after a fall with possible loss of consciousness?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: A 12-lead ECG (with lying and standing blood pressure).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: What is the significance of a head strike on anticoagulants?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: A high risk of intracranial haemorrhage — low threshold for a CT head.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: What examination finding indicates a neck-of-femur fracture after a fall?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: A shortened and externally rotated leg with hip pain and inability to weight-bear.
With lying and standing blood pressure (a sustained drop of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic on standing).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: What acute illnesses can present as a fall in the elderly?
What are the components of a multifactorial falls assessment?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back:
• Gait and balance
  • lying / standing BP
  • ECG
  • medication review
  • vision
  • cognition
  • continence
  • bone health
  • and home hazards.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.front: What intervention reduces recurrent falls in the community?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Falls.back: Strength and balance training (physiotherapy) plus addressing reversible factors and home hazards.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.back: It is a non-specific label that hides an unexamined cause; the task is always to find the medical, functional, cognitive or social reason for decline.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.front: How should an acute or subacute functional decline (“off legs”) be regarded?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.back:
As acute illness until proven otherwise —
  • sepsis
  • MI
  • stroke
  • AKI
  • delirium
  • or drug toxicity.
A state of reduced physiological reserve across multiple systems, leaving the person vulnerable to decompensation from minor stressors.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.front: What is delirium and how is it screened?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.back: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition; screened with the 4AT, with a search for the precipitant.
A multidimensional, multidisciplinary assessment of medical, functional, psychological and social domains with a coordinated care plan.
Age- and illness-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, contributing to frailty and functional decline.
By a structured medication review (e.g. STOPP-START) to stop harmful / unnecessary drugs and start indicated ones.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.front: Which reversible contributors to decline should always be sought?
What is the overall goal of managing frailty?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Frailty & Fun.back: To identify and treat reversible causes and to maintain / restore function through a multidisciplinary, goal-focused plan.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: What is a collapse / transient loss of consciousness (TLoC)?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: A spontaneous, self-limiting loss of consciousness with complete recovery; the aim is to distinguish cardiac syncope from neurological and reflex causes.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: Why is an ECG mandatory in every collapse?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: To detect life-threatening cardiac causes (arrhythmia, conduction disease, long QT, pre-excitation, ischaemia) that can cause sudden death.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: What are the red-flag features pointing to cardiac syncope?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back:
• Collapse on exertion
  • without warning
  • causing injury
  • a family history of sudden cardiac death
  • or an abnormal ECG.

With
  • a prodrome (nausea, sweating, tunnel vision)
  • a trigger (standing, pain, emotion)
  • and rapid, complete recovery.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: How is orthostatic hypotension identified as a cause?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: Collapse on standing with a documented postural drop in blood pressure (lying / standing BP).
Lateral tongue-biting, sustained (not brief) tonic-clonic movements and prolonged post-ictal confusion. Incontinence and brief jerks occur in syncope too, so they do not reliably distinguish the two.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: Which metabolic cause of collapse must be checked at the bedside?
What investigations are used to evaluate an unexplained collapse?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: Eyewitness history, 12-lead ECG, lying / standing BP, bloods / glucose, then echo, ambulatory ECG monitoring, CTPA or EEG as directed.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: What advice must accompany certain collapses regarding driving?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: DVLA rules apply — patients may need to stop driving and notify the DVLA depending on the cause and features.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.front: Why is an eyewitness account so valuable?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Unexplained C.back: It clarifies triggers, prodrome, duration, movements, colour and recovery, helping distinguish syncope, seizure and cardiac causes.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: What is the first distinction to make in oedema?
What are the three great causes of generalised oedema?
How does nephrotic syndrome present with oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: Periorbital and dependent oedema with frothy urine (heavy proteinuria) and hypoalbuminaemia.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: What features indicate cardiac failure as the cause of oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: Bilateral pitting oedema with orthopnoea, a raised JVP and lung crepitations; confirm with BNP and echo.

Reduced plasma oncotic pressure — from
  • malnutrition
  • nephrotic syndrome
  • liver disease
  • or protein loss.
Peripheral oedema with ascites and stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: Why must a unilateral hot swollen leg not be treated as systemic oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: It is likely a DVT needing a Doppler and anticoagulation (with PE risk), not diuretics.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: What urgent presentation is sudden facial and tongue swelling?
What core investigations sort out generalised oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: Urinalysis (protein) and urine protein:creatinine ratio, U&E, LFTs, serum albumin and BNP, with echo / renal / liver imaging.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: How does myxoedema differ from typical dependent oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: It is non-pitting (hypothyroidism), unlike the pitting oedema of cardiac / renal / hepatic causes.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.front: What is the general management principle for systemic oedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised /.back: Treat the overload (e.g. diuresis) and the underlying cause (cardiac, renal, hepatic or hypoalbuminaemic).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: How is the severity of fluid depletion assessed clinically?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back:
By
  • observations (HR, BP, postural drop)
  • mucous membranes
  • skin turgor
  • capillary refill
  • JVP
  • urine output
  • and urea.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: What is the emergency at the severe end of fluid depletion?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: Hypovolaemic shock — tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria and a raised lactate — needing immediate fluid resuscitation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: Which severe conditions cause large fluid deficits?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back:
• DKA / HHS
  • GI catastrophes (bleeding, obstruction)
  • and sepsis with distributive loss.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: What are the main GI causes of fluid depletion?
What are the renal / drug causes of fluid loss?
How does dehydration present in the frail elderly?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: As confusion with a raised urea and pre-renal acute kidney injury, often from reduced intake / dysphagia.
Sequestration of fluid into a non-functional compartment (e.g. pancreatitis, obstruction, sepsis, burns), causing intravascular depletion despite total-body fluid.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: How is diabetes insipidus suggested and confirmed?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: Polyuria with dilute urine and a normal glucose; confirmed with paired serum / urine osmolalities (water deprivation test).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: What blood picture supports a pre-renal (hypovolaemic) AKI?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: A disproportionately raised urea relative to creatinine (high urea:creatinine ratio) with concentrated urine.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: What is the initial management of hypovolaemic shock?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: A balanced crystalloid fluid challenge with reassessment, while identifying and controlling the source of loss.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: After resuscitation, how is fluid replacement planned?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back: Replace the estimated deficit plus ongoing losses plus maintenance, with the right fluid guided by electrolytes.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.front: Which bedside and laboratory tests guide fluid management?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dehydration &.back:
• Observations and urine output
  • U&E
  • glucose
  • a venous gas / lactate
  • and cause-directed tests (ketones, cortisol, osmolalities).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: A complex metabolic wasting syndrome — loss of skeletal muscle (with or without fat) driven by inflammatory cytokines — that is not fully reversed by nutritional support alone.
Starvation is reduced intake and is largely reversible with feeding; cachexia is inflammation-driven muscle loss that persists despite adequate nutrition.
Tuberculosis and HIV (HIV wasting syndrome); also chronic sepsis such as abscess, endocarditis or osteomyelitis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.front: What is organ-failure cachexia and why does it matter?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: Muscle wasting in advanced cardiac (heart failure), respiratory (COPD) or renal (CKD) disease; it is a marker of poor prognosis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.front: Which endocrine disorder causes wasting despite a preserved appetite?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: Hyperthyroidism (weight loss and muscle wasting with a normal or increased appetite).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.front: What is refeeding syndrome and why is it relevant in cachexia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: Dangerous falls in phosphate, potassium and magnesium (with fluid shifts) when a severely malnourished patient is fed too aggressively; feed cautiously with monitoring.
Sarcopenia is age-related loss of muscle mass and strength; cachexia is an inflammatory wasting syndrome secondary to a specific underlying disease — though they overlap.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.front: Why should cachexia never be dismissed as 'just old age'?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: Because it commonly signals occult malignancy or advanced organ failure that needs investigation and treatment.
Identify and treat the underlying cause, add MDT nutritional support (with refeeding precautions), and recognise it as a prognostic marker; nutrition alone rarely reverses it.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.front: Which pancreatic cancer presentation may underlie cachexia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cachexia.back: Painless obstructive jaundice with epigastric/back pain and marked weight loss.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: What is the first clinical question in generalised itch?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: Is there a primary rash? Itch with a rash is usually dermatological; itch without a rash (only excoriations) mandates a search for systemic disease.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: Which malignancies classically cause itch without a rash?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: Lymphoma (Hodgkin's — sometimes itch after alcohol) and polycythaemia vera (aquagenic itch after a warm bath); also leukaemia.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: What causes 'aquagenic' itch after a warm bath with a ruddy complexion?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: Itch (often of palms/soles) with jaundice, pale stools and dark urine; e.g. primary biliary cholangitis, biliary obstruction or pancreatic cancer.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: Which systemic (rash-free) causes of itch should be screened for?
Which nail sign supports iron deficiency as a cause of itch?
Which dermatological conditions cause itch WITH a rash?
What are the clinical clues to scabies?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back:
• Intense itch worse at night
  • burrows in the finger webs and flexures
  • and affected household contacts.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: Which blood tests screen the patient with rash-free generalised itch?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back:
• FBC + film
  • ferritin
  • U&E
  • LFTs
  • TFTs
  • glucose
  • LDH (± JAK2)
  • bilirubin fractionation
  • and a CXR.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: Name a drug class that commonly causes pruritus.
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: Opioids (also ACE inhibitors, statins and many others) — look for a temporal link to a new drug.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: How is itch managed symptomatically while the cause is sought?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: Emollients and antihistamines, plus cause-specific agents (e.g. colestyramine for cholestatic itch, gabapentinoids/phototherapy for uraemic itch).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.front: Why is persistent generalised itch without a rash a red flag?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Generalised I.back: It can be the first sign of lymphoma, polycythaemia or cholestatic malignancy, especially with weight loss, night sweats or jaundice.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: By tempo — acute (minutes to hours) versus chronic (weeks to months); acute breathlessness with hypoxia is an emergency.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: List the immediately life-threatening causes of acute breathlessness.
What are the signs of a tension pneumothorax and its immediate treatment?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: Sudden breathlessness, a unilateral silent chest, tracheal deviation and shock; treat with immediate needle/finger decompression.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: What is the immediate treatment of anaphylaxis causing breathlessness?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: Intramuscular adrenaline (plus high-flow oxygen, IV fluids, and removing the trigger).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: What target oxygen saturations are used in COPD, and why?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: 88–92% (using controlled oxygen), because of the risk of CO₂ retention and type 2 respiratory failure.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: Which acute breathlessness cause features orthopnoea, PND and pink frothy sputum?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: Deep sighing (Kussmaul) respiration compensating for metabolic acidosis, with ketones.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: Which first-line investigations are done for acute breathlessness?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: SpO₂ and ABG, ECG, CXR, bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, BNP, troponin, D-dimer where indicated) and peak flow/spirometry; CTPA/echo as guided.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: What does a 'silent chest' in acute asthma indicate?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: Life-threatening asthma (peri-arrest) — too little air movement to generate a wheeze; needs urgent senior/critical care input.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: Which chronic causes of breathlessness should be considered?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity causes exertional dyspnoea, with pallor and fatigue; confirmed on FBC.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.front: What immediate management applies to any hypoxic breathless patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Breathlessnes.back:
• Give controlled oxygen to target saturations
  • assess ABCDE
  • and treat the specific cause while escalating if critically hypoxic.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: What must be clarified first when a patient says they are 'dizzy'?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Whether they mean presyncope/light-headedness (feeling faint) or vertigo (an illusion of movement/spinning) — the two have different workups.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: Which features in presyncope mandate an urgent ECG and cardiac work-up?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Light-headedness that is exertional or occurs lying down, associated chest pain or palpitations, a family history of sudden cardiac death, or an abnormal ECG — these point to a cardiac cause (arrhythmia, outflow obstruction) rather than benign vasovagal presyncope.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: What are the dangerous cardiac causes of presyncope?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Arrhythmias (tachy- or bradyarrhythmia/heart block) and structural disease (aortic stenosis) — a red flag for sudden death.
Light-headedness on exertion, with palpitations or chest pain, or leading to collapse; needs an ECG, ambulatory monitoring and an echo.
Light-headedness on standing that resolves on sitting/lying; caused by drugs, dehydration or autonomic failure; confirmed by a lying/standing blood pressure.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: Which systemic causes of light-headedness must be screened for?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Sweating, tremor and light-headedness relieved by food, typically in a diabetic on insulin or a sulfonylurea; check a capillary glucose.
Lying/standing blood pressure, an ECG (± ambulatory monitor), a capillary glucose and an FBC; echo if structural heart disease is suspected.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: What features point to vertigo rather than presyncope?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: A true sense of spinning/room-moving with nausea and nystagmus — follow the vestibular/neurological pathway.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: How does a vasovagal (neurally mediated) presyncope typically present?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: A prodrome of warmth, nausea and greying vision, provoked by standing, pain or emotion; benign but recurrent.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: How is light-headedness from an occult GI bleed recognised?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Light-headedness with pallor and melaena; confirmed on FBC and by finding the bleeding source.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.front: What is the management principle for drug-induced postural hypotension?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Dizziness / L.back: Rationalise the culprit drugs (antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives) and treat the postural drop.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: What is cyanosis and at what level does it appear?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: A bluish discolouration of skin/mucous membranes appearing when there is more than about 50 g/L of deoxygenated haemoglobin.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: What is the key first split in assessing cyanosis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Central (blue tongue and lips, systemic hypoxaemia or abnormal haemoglobin) versus peripheral (blue extremities, poor local perfusion, normal tongue).
Systemic hypoxaemia (respiratory failure or a right-to-left cardiac shunt) or abnormal haemoglobin (methaemoglobinaemia).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: What causes peripheral cyanosis with a normal central colour and SpO₂?
How does methaemoglobinaemia present, and how is it treated?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Cyanosis with a low SpO₂ but a normal PaO₂, chocolate-brown blood, that does not correct with oxygen; caused by drugs (dapsone, nitrites); treated with methylene blue.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: How do polycythaemia and anaemia affect the visibility of cyanosis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Polycythaemia deepens cyanosis (more absolute deoxy-Hb); anaemia masks it (a very anaemic hypoxic patient may not look blue).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: A neonate cyanosed from birth or on crying suggests what?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Cyanotic congenital heart disease (a right-to-left shunt) until proven otherwise; assess with a hyperoxia test and echo.
SpO₂ and an ABG with co-oximetry (met-Hb, oxyhaemoglobin fraction), ECG, CXR, FBC; echo for a shunt and CTPA for PE.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: How is central cyanosis best examined for?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Inspecting the tongue and lips (central) versus the fingers/toes (peripheral) and measuring SpO₂.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: What is the immediate management of central cyanosis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Give oxygen, obtain an ABG, and escalate; treat the underlying cardiorespiratory cause.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.front: Why does cyanosis in methaemoglobinaemia not improve with oxygen?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Cyanosis.back: Because the haemoglobin is oxidised (ferric) and cannot carry oxygen normally; it requires methylene blue rather than oxygen alone.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: Loss of the normal nail-fold angle with a boggy, fluctuant nail bed and increased nail curvature (loss of Schamroth's window).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: What are the major cardiorespiratory causes of clubbing?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back:
• Lung cancer
  • bronchiectasis
  • ILD/pulmonary fibrosis
  • cystic fibrosis
  • cyanotic congenital heart disease
  • and infective endocarditis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: What are the GI/hepatic causes of clubbing?
Which malignancy is the key can't-miss cause of new clubbing?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: Lung cancer — especially in a smoker with weight loss, haemoptysis or cough.
Painful wrists/ankles with periostitis accompanying clubbing, strongly associated with underlying lung malignancy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: Which clubbing cause presents with fever, a new murmur and embolic signs?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: Infective endocarditis (splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots) — take blood cultures and echo.
By loss of Schamroth's window when opposing the nails of two fingers, and a fluctuant nail bed with increased nail curvature.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: Which respiratory disease with chronic productive cough and recurrent infection causes clubbing?
Which first-line investigation is done for new clubbing?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: A chest X-ray (then CT/HRCT as indicated), guided by the history.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: What is the significance of unilateral clubbing?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: It suggests a local vascular cause rather than a systemic disease.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.front: Why is clubbing described as 'a clue, not a diagnosis'?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Clubbing.back: Because it flags serious underlying cardiorespiratory, GI or hepatic disease that must be actively sought and treated.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: At the conjunctivae, palmar creases and tongue — skin colour alone is unreliable.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.front: What are the three broad explanations for pallor?
What does sudden pallor with tachycardia and hypotension indicate?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: Acute haemorrhage/shock until proven otherwise (GI bleed, trauma, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic) — resuscitate.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.front: Why must iron-deficiency anaemia not be blamed on diet without investigation?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: Because it may be caused by GI malignancy or another occult bleeding source that must be excluded (e.g. colonoscopy).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.front: What does pallor with bruising and recurrent infection suggest?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: Marrow failure/leukaemia — needs an urgent FBC and blood film.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.front: How is pallor from haemolytic anaemia recognised?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: Pallor with jaundice and splenomegaly; confirmed by reticulocytosis, raised LDH and a positive DAT (if immune).
FBC and blood film, ferritin/haematinics, reticulocytes; then a source search (e.g. OGD/colonoscopy for iron deficiency).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.front: Which gynaecological cause commonly produces iron-deficiency pallor in women?
What is the immediate management of pallor with shock from bleeding?
Why should pallor always be confirmed with an FBC before reassurance?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pallor.back: Because skin colour is unreliable; conjunctival/palmar pallor correlates better, and only an FBC objectively confirms anaemia.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back: Inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery relative to metabolic demand, causing cellular dysfunction.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.front: What are the four classes of shock?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back:
• Hypovolaemic
  • cardiogenic
  • distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic)
  • and obstructive (massive PE, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax).
Septic, anaphylactic and neurogenic shock — characterised by vasodilatation and often warm peripheries.
Massive PE, cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax — mechanical obstruction to the circulation.
Haemorrhage (trauma, GI bleed, ruptured AAA/ectopic) or non-haemorrhagic fluid loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, third-spacing).
Pump failure — a large MI, arrhythmia, or an acute valve/septal rupture; fluids can worsen it.
A raised lactate is an early marker of tissue hypoperfusion and helps recognise shock and monitor resuscitation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.front: What is the immediate treatment of septic shock?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back: The Sepsis 6 within the hour (oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.front: What is the immediate treatment of anaphylactic shock?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back: Intramuscular adrenaline, plus oxygen, IV fluids and removal of the trigger.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.front: How are the emergency treatments of obstructive shock matched to cause?
How can peripheral warmth help classify shock?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back: Warm peripheries suggest distributive shock; cold, clamped peripheries suggest hypovolaemic or cardiogenic shock.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.front: What is the general assessment framework for a shocked patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Shock (Classi.back: ABCDE with oxygen and IV access, bloods (FBC, U&E, lactate, cross-match, cultures, troponin), ECG and bedside echo/ultrasound to identify the type.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: What does 'off legs' mean and how should it be regarded?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: A sudden loss of mobility/independence in an older person; it should be treated as acute illness until proven otherwise.
They are non-diagnoses that risk missing serious, treatable acute illness such as sepsis, MI, stroke or fracture.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: What is the commonest hidden cause of an older person going off their legs?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: Sepsis, often from a urinary tract infection or pneumonia, sometimes with few localising signs.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: Which acute cardiac/neurological catastrophes present as 'off legs'?
Which metabolic/iatrogenic causes should be screened for?
Which occult injury must be excluded in an older person off their legs?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: A fractured neck of femur (a shortened, externally rotated leg) and other fractures.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: What bedside/blood screen is mandatory in 'off legs'?
How is cord compression suggested in a patient off their legs?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: Leg weakness with urinary retention and back pain — needs urgent MRI of the whole spine (within 24h if metastatic cord compression is suspected).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: Why can the frail elderly be septic without a fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: Blunted physiological responses mean sepsis may present only as a raised NEWS, new confusion or simply being 'off legs'.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: What tool screens for delirium in this presentation?
What is the management approach once the precipitant is found?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back:
• Treat the acute cause
  • rationalise culprit drugs
  • and rehabilitate with the MDT (physiotherapy, occupational therapy).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.front: What is the correct comprehensive assessment framework for the frail patient off their legs?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Off Legs / Ac.back: A comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA), not a dismissive label.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back: Localised skin and soft-tissue injury over a bony prominence caused by sustained pressure and shear.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: Where do pressure sores most commonly occur?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back: Category 1 (non-blanching erythema, intact skin) to category 4 (full-thickness with exposed bone/tendon/muscle), plus unstageable and deep-tissue injury.
Non-blanching erythema of intact skin over a bony prominence.
Full-thickness tissue loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: What is the dangerous infective complication of a pressure sore?
How is osteomyelitis suggested in a pressure ulcer?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back: A deep ulcer that probes to bone or fails to heal; confirmed by MRI or bone biopsy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: Which risk-assessment tools are used for pressure injury?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back: Surface (pressure-relieving), Skin inspection, Keep moving (repositioning), Incontinence care, and Nutrition — a prevention bundle.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: Why can pressure sores be a safeguarding issue?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back: Severe or multiple avoidable ulcers can be a marker of neglect and warrant a safeguarding referral.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: How are pressure ulcers distinguished from moisture lesions and leg ulcers?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back:
• Pressure ulcers occur over bony prominences from pressure/shear
  • moisture lesions arise from incontinence-associated dermatitis
  • leg ulcers have venous/arterial features at the ankle.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.front: What are the pillars of pressure sore management?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Pressure Sore.back:
• Relieve pressure
  • treat infection
  • optimise nutrition and perfusion
  • appropriate wound care/debridement
  • and safeguarding where neglect is suspected.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: Define hypothermia and how core temperature is measured.
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back: A core temperature below 35°C, measured with a low-reading thermometer.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: What classic ECG change is seen in hypothermia?
Why must the severely hypothermic patient be handled gently?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back: The cold myocardium is irritable and prone to ventricular fibrillation, which can be triggered by rough movement.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: What does 'not dead until warm and dead' mean?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back: Resuscitation should continue during rewarming, because signs of life may be undetectable and recovery is possible even after prolonged arrest in hypothermia.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: Which precipitants of hypothermia must be sought?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back: Hypothermia with drowsiness, slow-relaxing reflexes, a goitre and bradycardia (severe hypothyroidism).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: Which groups are most at risk of environmental hypothermia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back: The frail, elderly, immobile and those living alone; also those misusing alcohol/drugs and the homeless; and neonates.
A further fall in core temperature during rewarming as cold peripheral blood returns to the core.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.front: What are the rewarming strategies by severity?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hypothermia.back:
• Passive (blankets, warm environment)
  • active external (forced warm air)
  • and active internal (warm IV fluids, warmed humidified oxygen, lavage/ECMO in extremis).
Core temperature, ECG, glucose, U&E, TFTs, cortisol, FBC, CRP, cultures and a venous gas; CK after a long lie.
Because sepsis in the frail may present with hypothermia rather than fever; always septic-screen.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.back: Hyperthermia is a raised core temperature from failed thermoregulation (heat gain exceeds loss); fever is a regulated rise in set-point (e.g. from infection).
Heat exhaustion has a core below 40°C with sweating and intact cognition; heat stroke has a core above 40°C with CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.front: What is the immediate treatment of heat stroke?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.back: Rapid aggressive cooling (evaporative cooling or cold-water immersion, cooled fluids) and support of failing organs.
Hyperthermia with lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a raised CK, on antipsychotics; treat by stopping the drug, cooling, and dantrolene/bromocriptine.
Hyperthermia with clonus, hyperreflexia and agitation on serotonergic drugs; treat with supportive care and cyproheptadine.
A hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetics/suxamethonium, with rigidity and rising temperature/CO₂; treated with dantrolene.
Hyperthermia with atrial fibrillation, tremor, agitation and features of thyrotoxicosis; treated with beta-blockade, antithyroid drugs, iodine and steroids.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.front: Why must sepsis be distinguished from heat illness?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.back: Sepsis is a regulated fever with a different mechanism and treatment (Sepsis 6); it must not be confused with hyperthermia.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.front: What complications should be monitored for in severe hyperthermia?

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.back: Core temperature, drug history, CK, U&E, LFTs, coagulation, venous gas/lactate, TFTs, glucose, FBC and cultures; urine myoglobin.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.front: What is the general management principle for hyperthermia?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Hyperthermia.back:
• Cool rapidly
  • stop the culprit agent
  • give the specific antidote
  • and support failing organs.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: What defines a safeguarding concern in an adult at risk?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: A reasonable belief that an adult with care and support needs is experiencing, or is at risk of, abuse or neglect and is unable to protect themselves — triggering a duty to act under the Care Act 2014.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: What are the main categories of abuse?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back:
• Physical
  • neglect / acts of omission
  • self-neglect
  • financial or material
  • psychological / emotional
  • sexual
  • discriminatory
  • organisational (institutional)
  • domestic abuse
  • and modern slavery
(Care Act 2014).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: Which injury features suggest physical abuse rather than accident?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back:
• Patterned injuries (grip, ligature or slap marks)
  • injuries of different ages
  • injuries inconsistent with the explanation
  • and a delayed or changing history.
Pressure sores, dehydration, malnutrition, poor hygiene, missed medication, untreated illness and unsafe living conditions in a dependent adult.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: Why should a vulnerable adult be seen alone?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: A controlling carer or perpetrator may answer for the patient and prevent disclosure; seeing them alone allows a private, sensitive account in their own words.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: How should you document a possible abuse injury?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: Objectively and contemporaneously — the patient’s own words verbatim, body maps, measurements and, with consent, photographs; preserve any evidence.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: What is the role of mental capacity assessment in safeguarding?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: Capacity is decision-specific under the Mental Capacity Act; where a person lacks capacity, act in their best interests, and if they are deprived of their liberty use a DoLS authorisation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: Who do you refer a safeguarding concern to?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: The local authority adult safeguarding team under the Care Act 2014, involving the MDT, and the police if a crime is suspected.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: Does a clinician need to prove abuse before acting?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: No — you report a reasonable concern with the documented facts; the safeguarding process investigates and establishes what has happened.
Neglect and poor care arising from the routines, systems or culture of an institution such as a care home or hospital, rather than a single perpetrator.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: How should carer stress be approached when it contributes to harm?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back: Recognise and support the overwhelmed carer while still protecting the adult at risk — support and safeguarding are not mutually exclusive.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.front: What is financial abuse and how might it present?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Elder Abuse /.back:
The illegal or unauthorised use of a person’s money or property —
  • unexplained loss of funds
  • unpaid bills despite means
  • or a new contact controlling finances or coercing over a will.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: What are the components of the Sepsis 6?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: Three in — oxygen, IV fluids and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics; three out — blood cultures, serum lactate and urine-output monitoring; delivered within one hour.
Respiratory rate ≥22/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, and altered mentation (GCS <15); ≥2 flags a higher risk of poor outcome.
Sepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a MAP ≥65 mmHg and a serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: What is the significance of a raised lactate in sepsis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: It reflects tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, grades severity, and its clearance tracks the response to resuscitation.
Fever in a neutropenic patient (e.g. within weeks of chemotherapy) can deteriorate rapidly; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are given within one hour without waiting for the neutrophil count.
A non-blanching purpuric / petechial rash with fever — treat as meningococcal disease with immediate antibiotics.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: Why can the frail elderly be septic without a fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: A blunted physiological response means they may be normothermic or hypothermic; malaise, new confusion or a fall may be the only sign, so a low threshold and a lactate are needed.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: What does 'source control' mean in sepsis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: Physically eradicating the focus of infection — draining an abscess, removing an infected line, or relieving an obstruction — alongside antibiotics.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: Why should antibiotics not be delayed for imaging in sepsis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: Mortality rises with each hour of delay; empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are given promptly after cultures, and the source is then sought and controlled.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: Which tool is used to track deterioration and trigger escalation in a septic patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: NEWS2 (National Early Warning Score 2), which aggregates physiological observations and prompts escalation as the score rises.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.front: What common organ complication follows sepsis, and how is it monitored?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Sepsis / The.back: Acute kidney injury — monitored with urine output and serum creatinine / U&E.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: What is the single most important diagnosis to exclude in a febrile returning traveller?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Malaria — especially Plasmodium falciparum, which can be rapidly fatal.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: How is malaria diagnosed and why are repeat tests needed?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Thick and thin blood films (with a rapid antigen test); films are repeated up to three times, 12–24 hours apart, because a single negative film does not exclude malaria.
Fever with relative bradycardia, headache, abdominal symptoms (constipation or diarrhoea) and rose spots, typically after travel to the Indian subcontinent; confirmed by blood / stool culture.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: What are the classic features of dengue?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Fever, severe myalgia, retro-orbital pain, headache and rash with thrombocytopenia and leucopenia after a short incubation; confirmed by NS1 antigen / serology.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: Why is a viral haemorrhagic fever a public health emergency?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: It is highly transmissible and dangerous; a febrile patient with bleeding who has been in an endemic area within 21 days must be isolated, managed with strict infection control and notified before extensive sampling.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: How does the incubation period help narrow the differential?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back:
• Short (<10 days) suggests dengue, other arboviruses and early VHF
  • intermediate suggests typhoid and malaria
  • malaria and TB can present weeks to months later.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: Which travel-related causes of fever are associated with jaundice?
What must always be included when taking a travel history?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back:
• Itinerary and dates
  • rural vs urban exposure
  • freshwater / animal / insect / food / sexual contact
  • and malaria prophylaxis and vaccinations taken.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: Why should HIV be considered in a returning traveller with fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Acute HIV seroconversion causes a non-specific febrile illness, and travel may involve exposure risk; an HIV test is part of the workup.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: Which cosmopolitan causes of fever must not be forgotten in a traveller?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Common UK infections such as pneumonia and urinary tract infection, and any source of sepsis — travel does not exclude ordinary illness.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: What causes travellers’ diarrhoea and when is it concerning?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: Usually bacterial (e.g. enterotoxigenic E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella); concerning if there is blood, high fever, dehydration or persistence, prompting stool culture / microscopy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.front: Which region and feature classically point to typhoid rather than malaria?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever in the.back: The Indian subcontinent with relative bradycardia and rose spots points to typhoid, whereas sub-Saharan Africa with positive (or repeatedly needed) blood films points to malaria.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: Warning features that should prompt consideration of immunodeficiency — infections that are Severe, Persistent, Unusual or Recurrent.
Secondary immunodeficiency is far commoner (e.g. HIV, drugs, diabetes, malnutrition, hyposplenism, neutropenia, hypogammaglobulinaemia from myeloma or protein loss).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Recurrent infection with encapsulated bacteria suggests a defect in which arms of immunity?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: Antibody (humoral) immunity, splenic function or the complement system — all needed for opsonisation and clearance of encapsulated organisms.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Recurrent Neisseria (e.g. meningococcal) infections point to which deficiency?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: Terminal complement pathway deficiency (C5–C9 / membrane attack complex).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Which pattern of organism suggests a phagocyte defect such as chronic granulomatous disease?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: Recurrent catalase-positive bacterial (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) and fungal (e.g. Aspergillus) infections with abscesses and granulomas.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Opportunistic infections such as PCP, oesophageal candida and CMV suggest which defect?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: A T-cell (cell-mediated) immunodeficiency — most commonly HIV; test for HIV.

A primary antibody deficiency (hypogammaglobulinaemia with poor vaccine responses) presenting with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and bronchiectasis, often in adulthood; treated with immunoglobulin replacement.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Why is the asplenic / hyposplenic patient at particular risk?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back: They are prone to overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated bacteria, especially pneumococcus; they need vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.front: Which initial tests screen for immunodeficiency in recurrent infection?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Recurrent Inf.back:
• FBC with differential and film
  • HIV test
  • serum immunoglobulins with protein electrophoresis
  • complement (CH50 / AP50)
  • specific antibody / vaccine responses
  • and lymphocyte subsets.
Myeloma (and other lymphoproliferative disease) and protein loss (nephrotic syndrome or protein-losing enteropathy); also some drugs.
By a neutrophil oxidative (respiratory) burst test (e.g. dihydrorhodamine / DHR flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: A severe, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction with rapid-onset Airway, Breathing or Circulation problems, usually with skin and mucosal changes, after exposure to a trigger.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the first-line treatment of anaphylaxis and its adult dose?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: Intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: Why is adrenaline given IM rather than IV in most settings?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is rapidly effective and safe; IV adrenaline risks arrhythmia and is reserved for expert / critical-care settings (refractory anaphylaxis).
ABC management — high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus, and positioning (lie flat with legs raised for hypotension, or sit up if breathing is the main problem); call for help.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: What is the underlying mechanism of most anaphylaxis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: An IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity reaction causing mast-cell and basophil degranulation; non-IgE and idiopathic mechanisms also occur.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: What is a biphasic reaction and its implication for management?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: A recurrence of anaphylaxis hours after initial recovery (up to 72 hours); patients are observed (commonly 6–12 hours) before discharge.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: Which blood test helps confirm anaphylaxis retrospectively, and how is it taken?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back:
Mast cell tryptase, taken as timed samples —
  • at presentation
  • at 1–2 hours
  • and at ≥24 hours as a baseline.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: How is anaphylaxis distinguished from isolated urticaria or angioedema?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: Anaphylaxis has Airway, Breathing or Circulation compromise; isolated urticaria / angioedema without ABC involvement is not anaphylaxis and does not need adrenaline.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: What should every patient receive after an episode of anaphylaxis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back:
• Observation for a biphasic reaction
  • two adrenaline auto-injectors with training
  • a written emergency plan
  • and referral to a specialist allergy clinic.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: Why might a patient on a beta-blocker respond poorly to adrenaline?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: Beta-blockade can blunt the response to adrenaline; glucagon may be used in refractory cases.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.front: What is refractory anaphylaxis and how is it managed?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Anaphylaxis.back: Anaphylaxis not responding to two appropriate IM adrenaline doses; it is managed with an IV adrenaline infusion and critical-care support.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: What is the overall approach to the poisoned patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back:
• Resuscitate ABCDE first (with glucose and an ECG)
  • recognise the toxidrome
  • and consult TOXBASE / the National Poisons Information Service for specific antidotes and thresholds.
Pinpoint pupils (miosis), respiratory depression and reduced consciousness; reversed with naloxone while supporting the airway.
Hot, dry, flushed skin, dilated pupils (mydriasis), tachycardia, urinary retention, and delirium — ‘mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, red as a beetroot, hot as a hare’.
SLUDGE / DUMBELS (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis), miosis, bradycardia and bronchorrhoea (e.g. organophosphates); treated with atropine (± pralidoxime).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: How does the sympathomimetic toxidrome differ from the anticholinergic one?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: Both cause mydriasis, tachycardia and agitation, but sympathomimetics (cocaine, amphetamines) cause sweating (a wet skin), whereas anticholinergics cause a dry skin and urinary retention.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: Why is paracetamol overdose dangerous despite a well patient early on?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: It is often asymptomatic in the first 24 hours yet causes delayed, potentially fatal hepatotoxicity; management is guided by a timed paracetamol level on the treatment nomogram.
N-acetylcysteine, given according to the treatment nomogram (or empirically for staggered / unknown-timing overdoses).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: What are the features and treatment of tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: Anticholinergic effects, broad QRS, arrhythmias, hypotension and seizures; treated with IV sodium bicarbonate (and supportive care).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: What are the features of salicylate poisoning and its management?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: Tinnitus, hyperventilation and a mixed respiratory alkalosis / metabolic acidosis; managed with fluids, urinary alkalinisation and haemodialysis in severe cases.
The UK’s online clinical toxicology database (with the National Poisons Information Service) giving guidance on specific poisons, antidotes and thresholds.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: Which two bedside investigations must not be missed in any poisoned patient?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: Capillary blood glucose and a 12-lead ECG (assessing QRS and QT).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.front: Why is a psychosocial / risk assessment essential in deliberate self-poisoning?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Toxidromes /.back: Overdose may be an act of self-harm; assessing intent and mental state, and treating underlying depression, is part of management before discharge.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: A patient has a fever of 39°C, BP 85/50, heart rate 120 and lactate 4 mmol/L. What is the priority?
options: Initiate the Sepsis 6 within one hour
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: Fever with hypotension and a raised lactate is sepsis — the Sepsis 6 (cultures, lactate, urine output, oxygen, IV fluids, IV antibiotics) is delivered within one hour.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Which of these fevers meets the classic definition of PUO?
options: Fever >38.3°C for >3 weeks, undiagnosed after initial workup
Fever with an obvious chest source
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: PUO is a fever >38.3°C for >3 weeks that remains undiagnosed after appropriate initial investigation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: A febrile patient 10 days after chemotherapy has a neutrophil count of 0.3. What is the management?
options: Reassure and repeat count in a week
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour
Wait for culture results before treating
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: This is neutropenic sepsis — a medical emergency requiring empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: A young adult has a 6-week fever with painless rubbery cervical nodes, night sweats and 8 kg weight loss. Most likely?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: Fever with B symptoms and painless rubbery lymphadenopathy strongly suggests lymphoma; confirm with excision node biopsy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Fever with a new regurgitant murmur and splinter haemorrhages suggests:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: Fever, a new murmur and peripheral emboli / splinter haemorrhages indicate infective endocarditis — take blood cultures and arrange echocardiography.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Which is the single most important test in a febrile returning traveller from sub-Saharan Africa?
options: Thick and thin blood films for malaria
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: Fever after travel to an endemic area is malaria until excluded — send thick and thin blood films (repeated if negative).

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: A febrile patient develops a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. What should be given immediately?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: A non-blanching purpuric rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise — give parenteral antibiotics immediately.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Which is a recognised connective-tissue cause of PUO?
options: Adult-onset Still’s disease / giant cell arteritis
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: Autoimmune / inflammatory conditions such as adult-onset Still’s disease, giant cell arteritis and SLE are classic connective-tissue causes of PUO.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Why are empirical antibiotics generally avoided in a stable patient being worked up for PUO?
options: They can mask the diagnosis and delay it
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: In a stable PUO, blind antibiotics can partially treat and obscure the cause (e.g. culture-negative endocarditis); a systematic staged workup is preferred.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: An elderly nursing-home resident is drowsy and hypotensive but afebrile, with a raised lactate. This most likely represents:
options: Sepsis (the frail elderly may be septic without a fever)
Nothing serious as there is no fever
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: The frail elderly can be septic without mounting a fever; hypotension, drowsiness and a raised lactate should prompt full septic treatment.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Which test should be offered in essentially all patients with an unexplained persistent fever?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: An HIV test is a routine part of the PUO workup, as HIV and its associated infections / malignancies are important causes.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.question: Beyond first-line bloods and cultures, which imaging is particularly useful to localise an occult source in PUO?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Fever / Pyrex.explanation: PET-CT and cross-sectional imaging help localise occult infection, malignancy or inflammation to direct targeted biopsy in PUO.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: A 68-year-old has lost 7 kg over 4 months with a change in bowel habit and iron-deficiency anaemia. Best next step?
options: Urgent investigation / referral for colorectal cancer
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Weight loss with altered bowel habit and iron-deficiency anaemia is a colorectal cancer red flag needing urgent lower-GI investigation.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Weight loss despite an increased appetite, with a tremor and heat intolerance, suggests:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Weight loss with a good appetite plus heat intolerance and tremor is classic hyperthyroidism; confirm with TFTs.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: A thin 19-year-old woman has weight loss, amenorrhoea and a fear of gaining weight. Likely diagnosis?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Weight loss with a distorted body image, fear of weight gain and amenorrhoea in a young woman suggests anorexia nervosa.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Weight loss with steatorrhoea, bloating and a positive tissue transglutaminase antibody indicates:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Steatorrhoea and a positive tTG point to coeliac disease; confirm with duodenal biopsy.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: A patient with weight loss, drenching night sweats and a chronic productive cough should be tested for:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Weight loss, night sweats and a chronic cough raise tuberculosis — send sputum and a chest X-ray.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Which single test best screens for new diabetes as a cause of weight loss?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Osmotic weight loss with polyuria / polydipsia is screened for with glucose / HbA1c.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: A 40-year-old with weight loss, oral candidiasis and generalised lymphadenopathy should be offered:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Weight loss with opportunistic infection and lymphadenopathy warrants an HIV test.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: What is the minimum threshold of unintentional loss generally taken as significant?
options: Greater than 5% of body weight over 6–12 months
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Loss of >5% of body weight over 6–12 months is the usual threshold for significant unintentional weight loss.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Weight loss attributed to depression should only be diagnosed once:
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: A psychosocial cause such as depression is a diagnosis of exclusion — organic disease must first be ruled out.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Which is a feature of the malignant anorexia–cachexia syndrome?
signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.explanation: Anorexia–cachexia is a cytokine-driven metabolic state of wasting and anorexia not fully reversed by feeding.

signs__GENERAL / SYSTEMIC__Weight Loss.question: Which tool is used to screen nutritional risk in weight loss?
